Anytime something parses but does not compile, it is a bug in Stan. The debug mode is to diagnose run-time errors.

As far as I can tell, the cuts vector should be declared and populated in the transformed data block, rather than the transformed parameters block (and the same for anything else that is fixed). The compilation error happens when you try to divide by 70, and integer division is a bit fragile. I always do double division (i.e. / 70.0).

Ben

Integer division rules are simple, and follow programming
language conventions (C, C++ and Java, anyway):

(int/real) and (real/int) return real, promoting

It seems more likely that it would be a divide-by-zero issue,
which can arise due to the "zero" being underflowed.

For instance (not an example from your code),
it looks mathematically like 1 / exp(x) would never be NaN,
but if x < -800, then exp(x) = 0, and 1 / exp(x) == 1 /0 == NaN.

Extreme initializations can put you out in places where
the model underflows, especially if there's a lot of data that
tightly constrains the posterior --- values outside of that can
be ill behaved.

>

zBnc_YR[1] <- 1.0;
zBpec_YR[1] <- 1.0;
zBpcfc_YR[1] <- 1.0;
...


then you can save a lot of space and output by defining these
as transformed data rather than transformed parameters.

Also, if you have variables that you want to use for convenience
that you don't need in output, define them as local variables.

In general, when you have repeated subexpressions, such as
(1 - fic[1]) in:

V2[5 ] <- V1[5 ]*(1-fic[1])*(1-ff[2]) + V1[4]*(1-f0c)*ff[1];
V2[6 ] <- V1[5 ]*(1-fic[2])*(1-ff[3]) + V1[4]*(1-fic[1])*ff[2];

it's more efficient to define local variables rather than recomputing.
Each expression takes up space and requires time in auto-diff calc,
and re-using expressions allows the calculations and space to be shared.

When you have big sums, it's more efficient to define an array, assign
elements into the array, then all the sum() function. It saves memory
and time. That is, rewrite:

a <- b + c + d + e;

as:

{
vector[4] temp;
temp[1] <- b;
temp[2] <- c;
temp[3] <- d;
temp[4] <- e;
a <- sum(temp);
}

It seems like it'd be more expensive, but it involves fewer
operations (each of those + operations takes space and time,
whereas sum() is much more efficient). Allocation, loops and
assignment are very fast and minimally sized in R.

And please please use indentation and not something like this:

} ##### # # END OF QTR LOOP
} ##### # # END OF COHORT LOOP
} ##### # # END OF STATE LOOP (not implemented yet)

This:

for(j in 1:n_states) {
Bnc_ST[j] ~ normal( 0.0 , pri_sd ); } // state fixed effect

should be vectorized to:

Bnc_ST ~ normal(0, pri_sd);

Again, it does less memory allocation internally and is faster.

And don't ever do what you did in the same place in the code, which was:

for(j in 1:n_states) {
Bnc_ST[j] ~ normal( 0.0 , pri_sd ); } // state fixed effect
Bnc_AG1 ~ normal( 0.0 , pri_sd );

it makes it look like the Bnc_AG1 is in the loop! Indentation should
always always match the block structure.

Especially for programs this big, I'd recommend keeping the model
in a separate file. I'm constantly having to select and cut models
out of R strings to run them from the command line. And it keeps
the models outside of the code for a particular application.

This could be vectorized

for(j in 1:12) {
rrMort[j] ~ gamma( pri_mort[j,1] , pri_mort[j,2] ) ; }

by reversing order of indexing for pri_mort and writing

rrMort ~ gamma(pri_mort[1], pri_mort[2]);

- Bob

I've spent some time trying to decompose your model, but it's a bit too complicated for me to make a lot of progress (By progress, I mean verifying that the model is what you intended it to be.)

With that said, here's what I've learned:
  • There is no leak in the command line version. This is both under v1.3.0 and the current development branch.
    With that said, in some runs, the model is taking up to 12 GB, but it's not leaking. It typically runs at 141 MB on my machine for both v1.3.0 and the current development branch, when it thinks it's actually sampling.
  • This doesn't really tell us what's going on with the rstan version, but I don't think there's an actual leak.
  • I don't think the model is specified in a way that Stan can handle it. There's a lot of trickiness going on in the transformed parameters block and its showing up in the test gradient mode. From the command line v1.3.0, add the flag "--test_grad" and you can see that sometimes there are large differences between finite diff and the auto diff. Other times all gradients are nan. That's bad news. I was able to consistently get the nan's out by moving the transformed parameter tmp into a local variable, but that didn't really solve the underlying issue. The use of V1 and V2 in the transformed data block creeps me out a bit. It's just setting and resetting those variables too many times for me to be comfortable with it. The only difference in memory between runs in Stan should

instability Daniel was seeing in numerical evaluations.

Some of these problems we can't really fix at a deep level
because Stan lets you write arbitrary code and arbitrary code
with lots of numerical operations (like you have) can be
badly behaved.

I have been working on some complicated models over the past
couple of months and always start with the simplest model
we can, even if it doesn't make sense for the final problem.
It's easier to build up from things that work than it is to
diagnose something large that doesn't work.

It's usually good modeling practice to do this anyway because
it lets you compare the results of simpler models to more
complex ones.  (And no, I don't want to get dragged into

The question's really whether you get the same answer or
not. We haven't investigated this issue a lot ourselves
on NUTS.

Setting a max treedepth of 5 is still sound asymptotically (so is depth
0, which just reduces to Metropolis),
but it'll wind up being more of a random walk than with a deeper bound.

Generally, Matt and Michael (the ones who know the most about
this, along with Marcus) have been suggesting that you really
want to let NUTS go as far as it wants to, because that'll be
most efficient. Andrew, on the other hand, has argued for
lower upper limits. So depth 10 is something of a compromise.

The real question is how to verify that you're getting the
right answer. The danger's that you can get trapped in some
small region of the posterior and it can look like it's
converged (good R-hat and effective sample size estimates), but
it really hasn't. So if you can run with a deeper treedepth
and get the same answer, running with a shallower one should
be OK. Similarly, Michael's been suggesting all along to run
with a fixed lower step size than the one that adaptation finds
and make sure that provides the same answer.

- Bob

data {

data {
  int <lower=0> N;
  vector[4] ns[N];
}
parameters {
  simplex[4] B;
}
model {
  for (n in 1:N) {
    B ~ dirichlet(ns[n]);
  }
}

------------------------------------

transformed data {

    B ~ dirichlet(ns[n]);
  }
}

------------------------------------


First, notice the difference in data declaration. For multinomial, I've declared a 2D array of integers. For Dirichlet, it's a N-length array of 4-vectors.

Second, I've gotten rid of the transformed data block. Here, you want to declare the B's in the original model as a simplex. There's no need to try to do any trickiness -- Stan can handle it all under the hood for you.

If you wanted to try it out on more simple data first, you can replace the data block with a transformed data block like:

transformed data {
  int <lower=0> N;
  vector[4] ns[100];
  N <- 100;
  for (n in 1:100) {
    ns[n,1] <- 1;
    ns[n,2] <- 10;
    ns[n,3] <- 100;
    ns[n,4] <- 1000;
  }
}

Hopefully that helps and you can really simplify your model. If you want documentation on the distributions, you'll find them in the manual.

When we suggest breaking down your model, these are sort of the steps we take. Even with the Dirichlet example, I put in fake data (as shown), where I knew the expected parameter values. I had original swapped the parameters and the variables since I was working with the multinomial first (written as 'ns[n] ~ dirichlet(B)') and it was clearly not right. I wouldn't have been able to pick that out if I used the full dataset to begin with. I also wouldn't have been able to debug it as quickly if there were lots of things happening in transformation blocks or restrictive priors. I guess I don't have the ability to intuit parameters through a thick model.

Anyway, let us know how you get on with the rest of your model.

> and went with the current approach as there seemed to be some trickiness involved with the Dirichlet, in that (if I am
> interpreting the comments and the manual correctly), the Dirichlet should really be taking the counts */plus 1/* as its

> argument (i.e. if one had integer data, the likelihood of counts ~ Multinomial(theta) would be proportional to theta ~
> Dirichlet(counts+1)). I guess this extra step really is a trivial problem, but please confirm that this step (add one to
> the counts) is needed.

The Stan parameterization of the Dirichlet is the usual one:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_distribution

You can see from the density that if the parameter vector is
all 1 values, it's a uniform prior. So if you've seen 4 outcomes
of category 1, 3 of category 2 and 1 of category 3, and you
use a Dirichlet({1,1,1}) prior, then the posterior is
Dirichlet({5,4,2}), which is why I said the parameter is 1 plus
the prior number of observations in the doc.

> Also, do you know if Dirichlet will be vectorised in Stan 2.0? Presumably this would make Dirichlet the faster option
> as well.

Not yet. We're still working through the vectorization of
multivariates. The metaprogramming's tricky, so we've been putting
it off. But it's a high priority for us, so it'll be done soon
(by that, I mean probably over the next six months).

> For the transformed parameters section: I agree it is... busy. I need the detail to answer my research question, but
> there are many opportunities for bugs to come in. However, I have coded up a version in R and rcpp so will be able to
> use this to generate better inits (I think this has been a problem).

Reasonable inits help with convergence.

- Bob
